slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter three: the examination of the senses.

slides.heading: Who does the seeing?
points: Open your eyes: the room is there
The eye sees, the room is seen
Is there someone behind the eye?
slides.say: Open your eyes and the room is there: the window, the chair, the light on the wall. It seems obvious that the eye sees and the room is seen, and that somewhere behind the eye there is someone who does the seeing. The third chapter asks whether seeing can be found as a power the eye has on its own, and whether a seer can be found apart from the seeing.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Nine short verses
Tools from chapter 2: the three parts, doer and deed
The target: the six senses
slides.say: The chapter is short, nine verses, and it borrows its tools from the chapters before. The three-part analysis of chapter two returns, and so does the question of whether a doer is found apart from the deed. The target this time is the senses, the six faculties through which, for the Buddhist schools of Nagarjuna's time, all experience arrives.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
Nine verses
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Six faculties and their fields
points: Seeing, hearing, smell, taste, touch, mind
Each with its own field
For the Abhidharma, the eye's nature was to see
slides.say: Now the explanation. Verse three point one sets out the theory. There are six faculties: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and mind, which knows thoughts. Each has its field: sights for the eye, sounds for the ear, and so on. Here seeing means the eye as a power to see, not just the act. The Abhidharma treated these faculties as real elements, each with its own nature. The eye's nature was to see. Nagarjuna does not deny that we see. He asks what it would mean for seeing to be the eye's own nature, a power it carries around in itself.

slides.heading: Seeing does not see itself
slides.say: The first argument is famous and compressed. The eye does not see itself. Then how can it see anything else? At first this looks like a bad argument. A knife cuts bread without cutting itself. The point lies in the word own nature. If seeing were the eye's own nature, something it had by itself, it would have it in every circumstance, with or without an object, including when turned towards itself. An own nature cannot switch off. A nature that only shows up when there is something else to see is not the eye's own. It belongs to the meeting of eye, light and object. That is what the diagram shows. The opponent offers fire, which lights other things without lighting itself. Nagarjuna answers that fire's lighting has already been examined by the analysis of chapter two, and chapter seven returns to the lamp in detail.

slides.heading: Does seeing see?
points: Already seeing: 'sees' counts the act twice
Not seeing: what is not seeing does not see
An idle seeing is no seeing at all
slides.say: Verses four and five use the doubling argument from chapter two. Seeing sees sounds harmless. But either the seeing already sees, or it does not. If it already sees, adding sees counts the act twice, like the goer goes. If it does not see, it is not seeing, and what is not seeing does not see. Is there ever a seeing that is not engaged in seeing? No. An idle seeing, seeing nothing, is not a weaker seeing; it is no seeing at all. So seeing cannot be a thing that exists first and then sets about the act. It is named together with the act and with what it sees.

slides.heading: No seer apart from seeing
slides.say: Then the seer. Is there a seer bound up with seeing? Then the seer sees counts the seeing twice. Is there a seer apart from seeing? Then we have a seer who does not see, which is no seer. And if there is no seer, where are the seen and the seeing? The three stand or fall together. Seen means seen by someone. Seeing means someone's seeing of something. As the diagram shows, seer, seeing and seen are designated together, and the seer pictured as standing behind the eyes, looking out, is the one item never found. When you look at a tree, look for the looker. You find the tree, vivid, and the seeing of it, but no viewer standing apart from the view.

slides.heading: The chain that depends on seeing
slides.say: Verse three point seven quotes the Buddha: as a child is born in dependence on mother and father, consciousness arises in dependence on eye and form. Nagarjuna accepts this. Dependence is exactly his point. Verse eight draws the consequence. In the Buddhist account of experience, eye consciousness leads to contact, contact to feeling, feeling to craving, and craving to grasping, the links that keep suffering going. If seeing and seen are not found as things of their own, this chain has no self-standing first link, and grasping has nothing self-standing to hang from. This is good news. A chain of self-standing links could never be broken. A chain whose links arise only in dependence can be loosened at any point. Verse nine extends all of this to hearing, smell, taste, touch and thought.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: You still see the tree and hear the bird
Glasses still help
Seeing as a meeting of eye, light, object, attention
slides.say: You still see the tree and hear the bird. Eye doctors still test your sight, and glasses still help. In Chandrakirti's reading, the analysis refutes seeing that exists by its own nature, not the seeing the world knows. What goes is a picture: an eye that holds the power of sight inside it, an observer sitting behind it, and a world waiting outside. In its place is seeing as a meeting: eye, light, object and attention arising together, with seer, seeing and seen named from that one event.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Look at something near you
Look for a seer behind the seeing
Listen to a sound; look for a hearer
slides.say: Try it now. Look at something near you. Notice the seeing: colour, shape, distance, all at once. Look for a seer behind it. Then listen to a sound and look for a hearer. The sight and the sound are fully there. The one who supposedly receives them is not found.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Chapters 7 and 10
Anatta to Emptiness: The Great Desynchronization
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World, chapter seven, on the hard problem of consciousness, and chapter ten, on perceptual co-arising. In The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, the chapter on the great desynchronization explains why Nagarjuna's no seeing without a seer does not undo the insight of seeing without a seer. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter four, the examination of the aggregates.
